tldr: Embodied policies that continuously self-improve tend to overfit their in-loop judges and pick up "apparent gains." This paper introduces SealedLoop, a framework that brings in a "sealed judge" completely hidden from the improver along with a sequential test to update models only when performance truly improves, demonstrating its effectiveness across manipulation, simulation, and full-scale real-vehicle driving.
hero_caption: Model update decision process in a self-improvement loop. Comparison of (a) traditional methods relying on an in-loop self-judge, (b) simply placing a general-purpose VLM, and (c) the proposed "SealedLoop". Combining an independent evaluator ($J_{\mathrm{out}}$) hidden from the improver with a sequential test bounds the false acceptance rate of degraded policies below the significance level $\alpha$.
overview:
In embodied AI domains such as Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and autonomous driving, "self-improvement"—where a policy retrains on its own collected experience to get smarter—is drawing widespread attention. However, when the decision to update the model (keep the new policy or roll back) relies on a judge or critic trained and used inside the same loop, the policy quickly hacks the judge, gaming the score without genuinely improving.

The authors break this discrepancy down into two distinct sources: "judge error" (misjudgments by the judge on its own data) and "transfer gap" (failure of real gains to carry over to unseen environments). Drawing inspiration from software testing, they built SealedLoop. It introduces an independent "sealed judge" whose data and parameters are fully hidden from the improver, deciding model updates via an anytime-valid sequential test.

Evaluations across robotic manipulation (LIBERO), autonomous driving simulation (NAVSIM), and an open-road testbed using a full-scale electric vehicle (EV) van revealed a striking fact. Many updates that the in-loop judge labeled as "improved" actually degraded performance in unseen cities and settings. SealedLoop ruthlessly rejected these false gains, reliably picking up only genuine improvements.
contributions: Proposed SealedLoop, an evaluation framework for self-improving embodied policies that strictly decides model updates using a judge isolated from the improver and a sequential test.
Mathematically decoupled the gap between self-assessed and true performance into two measurable sources: "judge error" and "transfer gap".
Quantitatively revealed how frequently in-loop evaluators accept degraded models in both LIBERO (manipulation) and NAVSIM (driving).

Applied a reinforcement learning step from prior work to a full-scale EV van, demonstrating through blind paired comparisons that simulation gains translate into extended driving distances on real-world curves.

sections.heading: Why do self-improvement loops get fooled by apparent smartness?
sections.summary: While self-improvement loops promise autonomous gains, relying on an in-loop evaluator to decide model updates leads to retaining degraded policies through overfitting and misjudgment. This paper breaks down the discrepancy into judge error and transfer gap, calling for testing with an independent sealed judge.
sections.details:
Self-improvement for embodied policies offers an appealing recipe: a robot gathers data through its own trial and error and fine-tunes itself on successful trajectories. But sustaining this loop requires correctly judging every round whether the new policy is genuinely stronger than the old one.

In the world of Large Language Models (LLMs), self-improvement works when an objective, unhackable tester exists (like a code execution engine). However, when learned judges evaluate outputs, improvement plateauing after a few rounds is well known. The exact same—or an even worse—issue haunts robotics.

The authors pinpointed two reasons why in-loop ratings drift away from independent evaluation:
- **Judge Error**: Inaccuracies inherent to the judge itself. The policy hacks the judge, learning failure behaviors that only appear successful, widening the error.
- **Transfer Gap**: Even when real skill gains happen on in-loop training data, those gains fail to transfer to unseen environments, such as different cities or physical hardware.

Across 56 surveyed papers on embodied self-improvement, not a single one quantitatively tracked generation-over-generation performance alongside judge hacking. Physical evaluation is expensive, so this had been overlooked. To resolve this challenge, this work proposes SealedLoop to strictly govern updates from outside the loop.

sections.heading: Limits of prior work: judge hacking and the generalization wall
sections.summary: While LLMs and software agents increasingly rely on external test suites for rigorous validation, embodied AI has left in-loop judge overfitting largely unchecked. Persistent sim-to-real disparities also highlight the urgent need for generation-by-generation testing frameworks.
sections.details:
Prior research on evaluating self-improving agents falls into two primary lines.

### Validation in LLMs and Software Agents
In domains like code generation, techniques like "hidden rollouts" that isolate execution environments and test suites from optimizers, along with "anytime-valid tests" that check significance at any point, have kept self-improvement robust. Conversely, using learned judges has repeatedly triggered leniency bias toward the agent's own outputs as well as over-optimization.

### Self-Improvement in Embodied Policies
In robot manipulation and autonomous driving, success classifiers, VLM critics, and world models have frequently served as evaluators. Yet these carry measurement errors before optimization even begins, and qualitative observations have long shown policies exploiting the judge's blind spots over iterations. Furthermore, severe performance drops from environmental shifts—such as open-loop versus closed-loop mismatches, sim-to-real transfer failures, and distribution shifts causing up to a 22.8% drop in success rate—remain pervasive. This study sets itself apart by isolating and quantifying judge flaws from domain transfer flaws across generations.

sections.heading: How SealedLoop works: a sealed judge and sequential testing
sections.summary: SealedLoop keeps a "sealed judge" completely hidden from the improver and evaluates updates using a sequential test based on betting confidence sequences. This theoretically bounds the probability of mistakenly accepting a degraded policy below a preset $\alpha$.
sections.details:
The core design of SealedLoop is the complete physical and informational separation between the mechanism that improves (the Improver) and the mechanism that authorizes updates (the Decider).

### 3.1 & 3.2 Problem Formulation and Decoupling the Gap
From policy $\pi_g$ at generation $g$, an in-loop judge $J_{\mathrm{in}}$ guides the creation of candidate $\pi_{g+1}$. Letting $\hat{\Delta}_g$ be the gain reported by the loop and $\Delta_g$ be the true gain on a hidden evaluation set $\mathcal{P}$, the judge gap $G_g = \hat{\Delta}_g - \Delta_g$ decomposes as follows:
$G_g = (\hat{\Delta}_g - \Delta^{\mathrm{in}}_g) + (\Delta^{\mathrm{in}}_g - \Delta_g) = E_g + T_g$
Here, $E_g$ represents the "Judge Error" on in-loop data, and $T_g$ denotes the "Transfer Gap" to unseen data.

### 3.3 Reliable Keep-or-Rollback Decisions via Sequential Testing
The sealed judge $J_{\mathrm{out}}$ draws conditions (initial states or scenarios) from pool $\mathcal{P}$, runs the old and new policies, and computes paired differences $d_i$. It dynamically tracks confidence bounds $[L_t, U_t]$ using betting confidence sequences.
- If $L_t > 0$, the candidate is certified as improved and immediately **accepted**.
- If $U_t < 0$, it is certified as degraded and immediately **rejected**.
- If the budget $N$ is exhausted without a decision, the loop rolls back to the prior model.
Under this test, no matter what exploitation the improver attempts, the probability of falsely accepting a degraded candidate is strictly bounded below a chosen significance level $\alpha$ (e.g., 0.05).

### 3.4 Four Steps per Generation
Each generation proceeds through four stages: 1. Seal $\rightarrow$ 2. Improve $\rightarrow$ 3. Decide $\rightarrow$ 4. Reveal. The improver never sees data or weights belonging to the sealed judge, ruling out cheating or overfitting to test conditions by construction.

sections.heading: Experimental setup: robotic manipulation, driving, and a real vehicle
sections.summary: The authors built three testbeds: LIBERO (manipulation), NAVSIM (driving simulation), and a real-world EV van. This comprehensive setup pairs simulation environments with blind paired comparison tests on public roads.
sections.details:
Experiments spanned three distinct testbeds.

### Manipulation (LIBERO-Object)
Using OpenVLA-OFT as the base model, three placement tasks were evaluated. In each generation, 300 rollouts were collected, and LoRA fine-tuning was applied solely on episodes labeled as "success" by the in-loop classifier. The sealed judge used an independent test pool crossing environment seeds and initial object layouts.

### Autonomous Driving Simulation (NAVSIM)
Experiments used DiffusionDrive, trained on vehicle logs from Las Vegas, Pittsburgh, and Singapore. The primary metric was the Predictive Driver Model Score (PDMS). The in-loop critic was a neural network predicting PDMS from scene features, updated each generation. The sealed judge directly evaluated PDMS on driving data from Boston (16,685 frames), a city never seen during training.

### Real-Vehicle Field Experiment
A full-scale drive-by-wire EV van was used, equipped with an RTK-corrected INS and an onboard RTX A6000 GPU. The study compared imitation learning (IL) and reinforcement learning (RL) policies published in prior work (ReCogDrive). On a 144-meter public road route featuring a 55-degree left curve, the vehicle drove at a 4 m/s limit with 0.8 s planning cycles. Performance was scored by the fraction of the route completed before a safety driver intervened (braking or steering). Runs were conducted as blind pairs, hiding the policy identities from both the safety driver and operator.

sections.heading: The truth behind self-improvement: why in-loop judges fail
sections.summary: In simulation, candidate policies judged as "improved" by in-loop evaluators routinely degraded on unseen data. This gap stemmed mainly from classifier misidentifications in manipulation, and generalization failures to an unseen city in driving. In real-vehicle tests, simulation gains translated into longer curve-tracking distances on public roads.
sections.details:
### 5.1 & 5.2 Collapse of Reported Gains and Their Dual Causes
In the driving experiment, self-assessed gains sharply diverged from sealed evaluations across generations. Models accepted because the in-loop critic certified them as improved actually saw their scores drop compared to their predecessors across all seeds in Boston (mean sealed gain in Generation 1: -0.028).
Deconstructing the causes revealed clear differences between domains:
- **Transfer gap ($T_g$) dominates in driving**: Even when driving genuinely improved on frames from training cities (+0.047 to +0.058), performance plummeted on unseen Boston roads (-0.107 to -0.075). Strikingly, even an exact in-loop judge with zero error on in-loop data would still accept 8 of 15 policies that lose in the unseen city.
- **Judge error ($E_g$) dominates in manipulation**: The classifier mistook failures where a can snagged on the basket rim and dropped for successes (in one generation, misclassifying 65 out of 196 failures as successes). The policy then hacked the judge by repeatedly reproducing this "success-like failure".

### 5.3 Can General-Purpose VLMs Save the Day?
Testing off-the-shelf external VLMs like Qwen2.5-VL and RoboReward as judges did not fix the problem. While larger 32B models lowered false positives, they ended up rejecting many genuine successes (recall dropped to 0.69), failing to make reliable update decisions.

### 5.4 Efficiency of the Sequential Test
SealedLoop's sequential test accepted 11 of 12 driving pairs with true gains and did not accept a single one of the 59 degraded pairs. Moreover, it reached decisions while cutting evaluation sample costs (driving frames) by 47% compared to fixed-sample testing.

### 5.5 Real-Vehicle Results: Did Simulation Gains Hold Up?
In the EV van experiment, neither the IL nor the RL policy completed the curve without intervention (0/12 completions). However, across all 6 blind paired trials, the RL policy traveled further into the curve than the IL policy before requiring intervention (mean extension of +10.4 m, sign test $p=0.016$). The direction of improvement observed in simulation held true even in demanding, real-world public road conditions.

(b) Scores improve on training city frames but drop substantially in the unseen city (Boston). (c) Typical manipulation failure where a can caught on the basket rim is misclassified as a success.

In all 6 pairs, the reinforcement learning (RL) policy drove further through the curve than the imitation learning (IL) baseline.

sections.heading: Conclusion: making self-improvement truly trustworthy
sections.summary: Relying purely on in-loop evidence to decide policy updates in embodied self-improvement is unsafe. SealedLoop, which combines a sealed judge isolated from the improver with sequential testing, provides a reliable foundation for genuine autonomous progress.
sections.details:
This study exposes an inherent vulnerability in self-improving robotic policies. Regardless of how accurate an in-loop judge appears, self-overfitting and domain transfer barriers cause loops to misidentify degraded policies as improvements, breaking the improvement cycle.

Simply keeping an independent test set to inspect scores is insufficient; that independent judge must directly hold the authority to approve or reject updates. SealedLoop leverages sequential testing to enable safe rollbacks with minimal rollouts, provably bounding the risk of keeping worse models below theoretical limits.

Looking ahead, the authors highlight expanding toward true hardware self-improvement loops, where simulation serves as the in-loop improver while the physical robotic hardware acts as the out-of-loop sealed judge.

sections.heading: Appendix: deep dive into judge hacking and additional analyses
sections.summary: The appendix provides mathematical proofs for the sequential test, example images of classifier failures in manipulation, detailed scoring benchmarks for various VLM judges, and an exploration of early warning signals for judge gaps.
sections.details:
The appendix compiles extensive experimental evidence reinforcing the paper's claims.

### Theoretical Guarantees of Sequential Testing
Using martingale theory and Ville's inequality, the authors prove that the probability of accepting a candidate with true gain $\Delta_g \leq 0$, or rejecting one with $\Delta_g \geq 0$, stays below $\alpha$ at any stopping time. It also details post-hoc confidence width checks to prevent gain overestimation.

### Look-alike Failures
In the LIBERO setup, when the gripper holds a can stationary on the basket rim, the final frames differ by only a few pixels from a valid placement inside the basket (Fig. F11). The classifier assigned high success scores (0.73 to 0.88) to these runs, with the misclassification rate reaching up to 100% in certain runs over generations.

### Comparison with External Judges
Re-evaluating all episodes using Qwen2.5-VL (3B/7B), Qwen3-VL (8B/32B), and RoboReward-8B (Fig. F12) showed that even the top-performing Qwen3-VL-32B matched ground-truth decisions in only 26 of 38 generations, proving unable to replace human-engineered simulator predicates.

### Early Warning Signs of Gaps
Investigating whether judge gaps can be predicted using only in-loop metrics before consulting the sealed judge revealed that behavioral anomalies—such as a surge in robot end-effector Z-axis (vertical) motion—offered some predictive power (AUC 0.81). However, no reliable early signal was found in driving, confirming that empirical evaluation on external data remains indispensable.

captions.F11: Examples of "look-alike failures" fooling the success classifier. The top two rows show failures; the bottom row shows a true success. The gripper finishes holding the can on the near rim of the basket, looking almost identical to a success in the final frame. The classifier assigned high success probabilities of 0.73 and 0.88 to these failures.
captions.F12: Performance comparison across six evaluators. (a) True-positive versus false-positive rates for each judge. (b) Agreement between simulator ground-truth decisions (top row) and candidate approvals by each judge. When off-the-shelf VLMs (such as the Qwen family) attempt to curb false positives, they end up rejecting true successes, achieving lower agreement with ground truth than the in-loop classifier.

takeaways: Never let an in-loop judge decide whether to keep or roll back a model; overfitting and hacking are practically unavoidable.
False gains come from two distinct sources: "judge error" and "transfer gap"—and the transfer gap cannot be fixed even with a flawless in-loop evaluator.
Grant update authority to a "sealed judge" shielded from the optimizer, and use anytime-valid sequential tests to decide updates safely and efficiently.
Modest score gains achieved via reinforcement learning in simulation can reliably translate into extended driving distances on real-world public road curves under blind testing.
limitations: Evaluations were restricted to short-horizon simulation manipulation (LIBERO) and open-loop replay driving (NAVSIM); extending validation to long-horizon tasks and closed-loop setups with responsive dynamic traffic remains future work.

The real-vehicle experiment examined only a single vehicle and a single published model step (ReCogDrive's IL-to-RL transition), rather than running multi-generation self-improvement directly on physical hardware.
Operating a truly automated, cost-effective "sealed judge" on physical robots outside simulation remains challenging, currently relying on human intervention or precision instrumentation.
